source.title: UnStar: Unlearning with Self-Taught Anti-Sample Reasoning for LLMs
source.authors: Yash Sinha; Murari Mandal; Mohan S. Kankanhalli

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a different unlearning method and measures its performance under jailbreak attacks, bearing on whether prompting attacks recover targeted information.
record.gate_note: The paper reports normalized WPU scores for unlearning efficacy, model utility, and adversarial robustness. Its Harry Potter paraphrases are used in the unlearning procedure, so the reported outputs are not an independent prompting-only recovery attack. No fine-tuning recovery attack, activation edit or ablation, or quantization attack is tested.
record.test_reason: This is a new-method paper (UnSTAR). Its one result bearing on the claim is an adversarial-robustness score: the minimum unlearning efficacy under two jailbreak attacks, on Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 with the WPU dataset, compared against 8 baselines. Every score is normalized to the best method (=100). So it shows ranking, not absolute recovery or near-chance accuracy. That makes the evidence on E and F weak. There is no fine-tuning, activation-edit or quantization attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that anti-samples with misleading rationales enable targeted and fine-grained unlearning that keeps related knowledge, which prior methods cannot. The robustness claim ('excels in resisting adversarial attacks') appears only in the results section, not the conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: UnSTAR fine-tunes on generated paraphrases, incorrect answers, and misleading rationales, while preserving retain-set answers; this differs from the cited gradient-ascent, WHP, and related unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The robustness score is defined using the minimum unlearning efficacy under two jailbreak attacks; attack-specific scores are not reported.
record.problems: Experiments use Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 on WPU; normalized scores are not raw accuracies or recovery rates. Adversarial robustness is aggregated as the minimum across two jailbreak attacks, with no attack-specific results or uncertainty reported. Generalization beyond this model and dataset is not shown.
record.rows_left_out: No separately stated result values were omitted. Other Figure 2 metrics are not recorded because they do not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Absolute target accuracy relative to chance and absolute utility retention; only normalized scores are given.
Entirely untested: no ablation or access-versus-deletion analysis.
Not tested: rephrasing as an independent attack (the paraphrases were used in training), other languages, in-context information. Results for the individual jailbreak attacks are not reported.
Resistance to fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization and non-jailbreak prompting attacks.

missing.what: After UnSTAR, the model gives no correct answer to about 100 paraphrased Harry Potter questions. These paraphrases were the training anti-samples, so this is not an independent rephrasing attack.
Unlearning efficacy rises over about 100 iterations of paraphrase unlearning

record.verdict_notes: The record's E 'challenges' label (R9–R10, from normalized scores read as reversed) was dropped: normalized minimum efficacy cannot show absence of recovery. There are no A verdicts because all A rows are normalized and cannot show near-chance accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: The reported normalized composite scores do not establish targeted accuracy near chance or provide an absolute general-ability comparison; attack resistance is recorded under E and F.
No post-unlearning relearning attack using a small set of unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access blocking versus deletion is reported.
The study evaluates two jailbreak attacks through an aggregate adversarial-robustness measure; it does not separately test rephrasing as an attack, other languages, or in-context information.
The reported robustness evaluation covers two jailbreak attacks, not fine-tuning recovery, activation edits, quantization, or all prompting attacks named in the claim.

source_check.notes: Robustness = minimum unlearning efficacy under two jailbreaks, normalized to the best method (GA=100) and averaged over 5 WPU sets. There is no raw leakage rate and no unattacked comparison. The text names Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 only for 'our approach' and does not say separately which model the baselines ran on. It copies RWHP's settings. The Fig. 2 layout is lost in the text, and the text is arXiv v1. The appendix judge prompts are quoted and do not count as instructions.
